Mārcus. — Accipiō abs<sup>5</sup> tē libenter. Prō quō vulgus<sup>6</sup> «Praestōlor<sup>7</sup>!» dīcit.
Equidem<sup>8</sup> nōn recūsō. Nihil tuā causā recūsābō.
Appius. — Tū deinde cēterīs propīnā.
Mārcus. — Tite, praebibō<sup>9</sup> tibi dīmidiam pateram!
Titus. — Precor<sup>10</sup> ut tibi bonō sit. Sit tibi bonum atque commodum.
Prōsit tibi! (Prōficiat<sup>11</sup> dūrius dīcitur).
Appius. — Sed cūr cessat<sup>12</sup> patera? Cūr nōn obambulat<sup>13</sup>?
Dēficit nōs vīnum<sup>14</sup>? Ubi sunt oculī tuī, puer? Vola, affer ejusdem generis sextāriōs duōs!

Dispeream nisi saepe pudet mē prōdīre in pūblicum, cum videō quam cultae sint aliae...
quae multō pauperiōribus<sup>19</sup> nūpsēre<sup>20</sup> marītīs.

english: Appius. — So let each one finish his glass. You will [follow my example] (take from me the example). I drink this to your health, Marcus!
Marcus. — I accept it willingly from you. [For which] (in exchange for which) the people say «I'm waiting!».
As for me, I don't refuse. I will refuse nothing [because of you] (for your cause).
Appius. — You next, [drink to the health of] the others.
Marcus. — Titus, I drink to your health half a cup!
Titus. — I pray that it may be [for your good] (good for you). May it be good and favourable to you.
Your health! (Your success! one says more coarsely).
Appius. — But why is the cup stopping? Why isn't it going round?
Is the wine running out [on us]? Where are your eyes, boy? Quick (fly), bring two pints of the same kind!
Delia. — I [would rather] (would want) have married [any old idiot] (a mushroom), rather than [to have] married my Marcus.
Cynthia. — Why so, [may I ask]? [Have things] gone wrong (agreed) so quickly between you?
Delia. — And it [will never go well] (will agree) with such a man. You see how shabbily dressed I am! [That's how] (thus) he lets his wife go out (of the house).
May I perish if I am not often ashamed to go out in public, when I see how elegant the others are...
who have married much poorer husbands.

footnotes: Prosum, to be useful = pro + sum; conjugated like sum, but adding a d to the 2nd and 3rd persons of the singular of the present indicative (prodes, prodest), to the infinitive (prodesse), to the imperfect (proderam, prodessem) and to the future indicative (prodero). As with other verbs, the series of the PERFECTUM poses no problem (profui, profueram, etc.). Prosim, -sis, -sit, etc., present subjunctive; prosit, literally, may it profit, here, your health! (as in German).
Ebibere, to drink completely (bibere).

Quisque, each one; here in the nominative (subject of ebibat); f. quaeque, n. quidque. Suum refers to calicem (calix, -icis, m.): the adjective is often separated from the noun to which it refers by another word (here quisque), which makes it possible to accentuate the relief of the expression by a symmetrical construction.
Propinare + dat., to drink to the health of...
Abs = ab (or a before a consonant).

Vulgus, -i, n., the people, the crowd; although it belongs to the 2nd declension and ends in us, this noun is NEUTER: the accusative therefore remains vulgus. Not used in the plural. Derivative: vulgaris, -is, -e, vulgar.
Praestolari, to wait; from praesto = prae + sto, to stand in front. This verb is little used.
Equidem = ego quidem, as for me.
Praebibere: another compound of bibere (vid. sup. N. 2).
Precari, to pray.
Proficere: compound of facere.
Cessare, to delay, to slow down.
Obambulare: the prefix ob- gives the idea of going in front of...

Deficit nos vinum: deficit is construed with the accusative (nos). Another example: pecunia Juliam deficit, Julie is short of money (w. f. w., money abandons Julie...). Note the difference between deficere, which expresses a new state, and deesse, to lack, which expresses a permanent state.
Nubere + dative: vid. sup. L. 43, N. 16.
Fungus, -i, m., literally: mushroom. If need be, note the value of this word as an insult!
Nec unquam = et nunquam.
Patior, -eris, -i, passus sum, to suffer. Think of the Passion.
Multo pauperioribus: in front of a comparative, adverbs of quantity (multum, parvum, etc.) become multo, parvo, etc.
Nupsere: this is the other form of the perfect indicative 3rd person plural (instead of nupserunt).
comments: ERASMUS, Dutch scholar, man of letters and philosopher (1467-1536). He contributed to the revival of Latin which, as you have been able to notice, had hardly improved since the barbarian invasions.

Febris, tussis, vis have the accusative singular in im and the ablative singular in i. — Mordeo, -es, -ere, momordi, morsum. — Diu, adv., for a long time; comparative diutius; superlative diutissime. — Locupletare (from locuples, -etis), adj., rich.
To finish this lesson, it would be a good idea for you to revise the IMPERATIVE by consulting the grammatical appendix, § 24.
And do not forget the 2nd wave. Today lesson no. 12.

latin: Quod vīnum bibere vīs, ātrum an album?
Ātrum mālō. Album enim crūditātem creat.
Mēlius est tē aquam medicātam bibere.
Quid dīxistī? Nōn aegrōtō nec ūllam medicīnam sūmere cupiō.
Tē fortūna juvat, ego multīs morbīs labōrō.
Saepe cum febrī jaceō; raucā tussī tussiō.
Arthrīticus et podagrōsus sum.
Tōtā cute prūriō.
Ā cane rabidō morsus sum. Canis rabidus mē momordit.
Quī semper aegrōtant diūtissimē vīvunt.
Quī aegrōtī sibi semper videntur medicōs pharmacopōlāsque locuplētant.
latinAccented: Quod vīnum bíbere vīs, ātrum an album?

Mḗlius est tē aquam medicā́tam bíbere.
Quid dīxístī? Nōn aegrṓtō nec ūllam medicī́nam sū́mere cúpiō.
Tē fortū́na juvat, ego multīs morbīs labṓrō.
Saepe cum febrī jáceō; raucā tussī tússiō.
Arthrī́ticus et podagrṓsus sum.
Tōtā cute prū́riō.
Ā cane rábidō morsus sum. Canis rábidus mē momórdit.
Quī semper aegrṓtant diūtíssimē vīvunt.
Quī aegrṓtī sibi semper vidéntur médicōs pharmacopōlā́sque locuplḗtant.
english: What wine do you want to drink, [red] (dark black) or white?
I prefer red. White, in fact, [gives me indigestion] (creates heartburn).
It would be better for you to drink [mineral] (medicinal) water.
What did you say? I'm not ill and I don't want to take any medicine.
[You're lucky] (fortune helps you), I suffer from many illnesses.
I am often in bed with a fever; I have a hoarse cough.
I suffer from arthritis and gout.
I itch (all over) (on all my skin).
I was bitten by a rabid dog. A rabid dog bit me.
[People] who are always ill live a very long time.
Hypochondriacs (those who always seem ill to themselves) enrich doctors and pharmacists.
